prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock rests on one simple, general mechanism: at the magic wavelength the light shift cancels to first order, so thousands of atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime without Doppler or recoil shifts. That is the kind of clean idea I trust, and it is understood quantitatively. Several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) now reach roughly 1e-18 and compare clocks against each other. The results include gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, tests of varying constants, and a live discussion of redefining the second. The credit is also cleaner than for most of my other candidates. Katori made the proposal and early strontium demonstrations, and Ye drove the accuracy and many-body frontier, so two names fit an invention-plus-realisation prize. Seven of eight colleagues ranked this candidate, which is breadth I should not dismiss. I weigh the scientific argument on its own terms, and on those terms it holds. After reading the openings I place it above my own first choice, B057, mainly because B057 has a real attribution gap and B012 does not.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the lineage. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb that Ye's clocks depend on, and the 2012 prize covered quantum control of single ions, so a skeptic can call this an incremental continuation of recognised metrology. Ion clocks reach comparable accuracy, and Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley are not in the credited names. Metrology is also a tool rather than a discovery about nature. The promised payoffs (geodesy, dark-matter searches, an SI redefinition) are still in progress, and a prize might be better timed after the redefinition.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B012 first because the magic-wavelength idea is a clean, first-principles-understood route to extreme precision, and because the 2005 comb prize honoured a distinct earlier step.
responses.response: I agree on the mechanism and have moved up to it from fifth place in my opening ballot. I would qualify the claim that the 2005 prize is simply a distinct step. The Ye clock is a comb-referenced instrument, so the citation should state what is new: the neutral-atom lattice with its magic-wavelength cancellation and its many-body systematics. It should not read as precision metrology in general. I also suggest the committee ask whether the ion-clock community is excluded by the citation wording. I think it is not, because the claim is about the lattice architecture.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B012 fifth and raises the point that waiting for the redefinition of the second might be wise, as well as overlap with earlier comb and ion-clock recognition.
responses.response: I took the waiting argument seriously because I raised it myself. I now think it conflates a metrological decision with the scientific criterion. The physics (agreement between independent clocks at 1e-18, measured redshifts over millimetres) is already established, and the Nobel criterion does not depend on a standards-body vote. Waiting would tie the prize to a timetable the committee does not control. I do still think her instinct to check the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is correct, and I would want that reflected in the citation.

responses.point: Eriksson places magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first: a theoretical flat-band prediction confirmed experimentally, opening a large and timely field of correlated moire matter, with theory paired to Jarillo-Herrero's experiment.
responses.response: I ranked B036 second myself and agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiment is the most striking theory-experiment pairing on the list. My reservation is about interpretation. The pairing mechanism is still debated, the correlated phases are not understood to the degree I would want for a prize, and Cao, Fatemi, Dean and others sit awkwardly around the credited trio. In the lattice clock we know why it works, whereas in moire graphene we know that it works. I would keep B036 as a strong alternative and revisit it in a few years, but I would not make it the lead candidate now.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B057 third and sees it as workable but incomplete, because the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is not in the credited names.
responses.response: This is the decisive point for me against my own opening first choice. I put B057 first because Z2 order is a clean universal mechanism with a measured edge conductance. But a three-name prize for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leaves out the people who proposed HgTe, and the Kane-Mele graphene gap is far too small for their original material proposal to have worked. Together with the overlap with the 2016 topological-phase prize, I judge that B057 carries a larger attribution risk than I accepted earlier. I still think it is scientifically deeper than the clock, so I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B012 first as a measurement method that opens new observation, and treats the missing credit for Lemonde and the ion-clock groups as a minor issue.
responses.response: I share the framing of the clock as a field-opening measurement method, and I accept that two names are enough. I think calling Lemonde and Hg-clock priority minor is a bit generous. Lemonde's group worked on the magic-wavelength concept in parallel, and the committee should look at the early record, around 2001 to 2005, before fixing the citation. This does not change my preference, but it is the main item to verify before a final ballot.

uncertainties: How much the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize reduce the novelty of lattice clocks in the eyes of the full committee.
Early priority for magic-wavelength trapping and lattice clocks among Katori, Lemonde, Ye and others; I rely on recollection.
Whether B057 can be given a fairer attribution set that includes the HgTe prediction, which might raise it above the clock.
Whether the pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene will be settled soon enough for B036 to overtake the clock.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B012: I have no collaboration with Katori or Ye. My Gothenburg environment is close to the Chalmers community of Johansson and Olsson, but I know of no personal collaboration with any credited candidate. I have no tie to B057 or B036 candidates either.
